data.title: What should the crypto industry know after the Democrats win Congress?
data.description:
Author: Bankless Source: X, @Bankless Translation: Shan Ouba, Jinse Finance

Two weeks ago, when the Democrats swept Congress, the crypto market initially didn't take it seriously, and Bitcoin quickly rebounded to above $79,000. But the good times didn't last long. This round of decline can't be largely attributed to Washington, but when AI turmoil and interest rate hike concerns dragged down the market, Democratic control of Congress went from "something the industry could weather" to "another thing to worry about."

So what exactly will the Democrats do? In a podcast released on Monday, Justin Slaughter, senior advisor at Paradigm and former legal counsel for the Democratic Congressional Oversight Committee, told David Hoffman that the next two years will be tougher, but it won't be like 2023.

He believes Democrats are angrier, busier, and more internally divided; the term "crackdown" doesn't adequately describe their approach. **Focus on Trump first, then discuss confrontation** **The investigations we touted before the election are still underway. Slaughter has heard they want to review SEC cases dismissed during Trump's presidency; he believes World Liberty and anything related to pardons will also be on their radar.** **But crypto won't be the only target. The oversight agenda he describes also covers AI, prediction markets, private equity, tariffs, and agriculture. Democrats have more pressing goals (I do think AI and prediction markets are priorities), and they don't have the resources to pursue all directions simultaneously.** How far the investigation can go depends on how the caucuses define what Trump represents. Slaughter believes this is the biggest unknown:
  • Trump is the problem itself: the scope of oversight remains "Trump and his affiliated companies."
  • Trump is the symptom: the scope of oversight expands, "potentially finding anyone, any company."

He gave this debate six months.

The central figure is likely to be Senate Banking Committee Chair Elizabeth Warren, though he remains optimistic that her influence within the party is not as strong as it was in 2021, despite "she still has a lot of support." He says most newly elected senators are more concerned with bringing prices down, and hearings rarely achieve that. He anticipates a period of "extensive oversight and trial and error," but cautions that, with very few exceptions, Congress ultimately follows the polls. **Regulator-Friendly, Why Isn't That Enough?** **A convenient and comfortable response is: as long as Paul Atkins is still at the SEC and Michael Selig is still at the CFTC, it doesn't matter. Slaughter says this is largely true, but "rules are not laws."**

Regulatory bodies can write rules, and the next batch of regulators can rewrite them. Congress can also insert supplementary clauses into appropriations bills to prohibit an agency from spending money on a particular rule—although Slaughter doesn't think crypto will encounter this. Furthermore, rules finalized at the end of an administration can be overturned through the Congressional Review Act. Revoking legislation is much more difficult, so even with worse conditions, Slaughter still wants a bill.

And the bill seems to be on its way. According to Slaughter and Eleanor Terrett, Maxine Waters is preparing a market structure bill that is stricter on DeFi and gives the SEC more power. But it's not all bad news: the bill may include industry-acceptable provisions, such as monthly proof of reserves and 24-hour withdrawals.

As for Warren, Slaughter suspects she doesn't want any legislation at all. In Democratic jargon Now, any legislation has to get past the Democrats. To get their votes, the industry has to change its rhetoric. Slaughter recalls a conversation with a candidate last year. The candidate was surprised to hear that stablecoins could reduce consumer costs and asked, "Then why don't you talk about that?" Slaughter believes that starting with decentralization misses the mark for a results-oriented party. Remittances are where digital data is most solid. World Bank data shows that in the third quarter of 2025, the average cost of remitting $200 overseas would be 6.36%, while using a bank would cost nearly 15%. An IMF study last month calculated that the average cost of sending the same amount of money via stablecoins across 270 payment corridors would be 2.18%, assuming the remitter chooses the cheapest exchange channel. Not every channel is cheaper, but for immigrant families, this difference represents real money.

However, the evidence weakens beyond remittances. Stripe's own case study shows that a merchant's cost of accepting stablecoins is 1.5%, while international credit cards cost 4.5%, yet there is no evidence that this saving is passed on to consumers.

As an industry, clarifying "how the saved money reaches consumers" is a good start. This argument may have a larger audience than it seems. Slaughter believes an overwhelming victory is better than a narrow one because it would attract more moderates unrelated to old crypto debates, such as James Talarico—who voted for Texas's strategic Bitcoin reserve when he was a state legislator. Some new faces are already talking about the costs. Michigan progressive Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed is not a recognized crypto ally (Slaughter says he's unaware of his views), but he argued in April that blockchain could simultaneously reduce the cost and waiting time of overseas remittances, provided Washington builds genuine safeguards. Even prominent crypto critic Sherrod Brown acknowledges that crypto is already part of the economy. The industry needs to amplify these arguments.

This kind of weight cannot come from campaign checks—and that's precisely where the industry has repeatedly stumbled. Brown was targeted by crypto PACs in two consecutive elections, and Juliana Stratton in Illinois received approximately $10 million in funding from crypto PACs in the primary; both won in November. While volunteering for a congressional election, I saw how easily the "dirty money" of super PACs can be equated with crypto, and how easily it can be seen as the same manipulative corporate force—and this midterm election is, to a large extent, a counterattack against that force.

A War of Attrition

Slaughter's bottom line is: using a two-year scoreboard is fundamentally flawed. He believes the real battle over crypto's place in the Democratic Party's eyes will unfold in the presidential primaries—which he says will be "about six months from now"—and he anticipates the next nominee will view Biden's approach as flawed.

Until then, the industry can hold on. The key is how to use this time: demonstrate that the technology can reduce costs, is non-partisan, and help politicians distinguish between "crime" and "crypto."

This likely also means cutting back on political spending, which is easier said than done.

Unfortunately, money is what gets politicians to listen to you. This cycle also shows that money can make politicians incredibly difficult to work with. "I don't want this industry to become completely at the mercy of the election calendar," Slaughter said. The Republicans gave crypto two good years; for it to continue, it depends on the Democrats. Author @davewardonline, originally published on Bankless Newsletter.

data.title: Nvidia Q3 Earnings Report: Understanding the Details Behind the Numbers
data.description:
Author: blocmates Source: X, @blocmates Translation: Shan Ouba, Jinse Finance

Nvidia just released its third-quarter earnings report. Unfortunately, there's not much new gossip to discuss in this report, but there are some very interesting details that we believe are worth your time to read.

Let's get started.

First, let's look at the core data:

  • Revenue jumped from $96.2 billion in the second quarter to $115.8 billion in the third quarter, a significant 20% increase quarter-over-quarter.
    • The data center business now accounts for 93% of Nvidia's revenue, contributing $107.6 billion. Shareholder returns: $28.1 billion returned through share buybacks and dividends. Remaining buyback authorizations: $227.3 billion. Operating profit: $77.5 billion, a year-over-year increase of 115%. Gross margin under pressure: Q3 reported 74.8% (down 0.2% sequentially), expected to decline to 71%–72% in Q4. Besides these headline figures, there are two other important highlights in this Q3 earnings report.

    Shifting to Infrastructure

    As the revenue structure shows, Nvidia is transforming from a pure GPU company into a full-stack AI infrastructure company.

    The future of the company increasingly depends on:
    • Capital expenditure of hyperscale cloud vendors
    • Adoption of enterprise-grade AI
    • Inference needs
    • AI agent deployment
    • Sovereign AI infrastructure

    This shift is also evident in a series of collaborations announced in the financial report:

    • Vera CPU: Custom CPUs for AI infrastructure.
    • NVLink Fusion: Connecting NVIDIA's infrastructure to custom XPUs.
    • Spectrum-X: Network infrastructure.
    • BlueField-4: Data processing and infrastructure security.
    • DSX POD: Complete AI Factory Reference Design.
    • OpenShell: Infrastructure for the Operation and Security of AI Agents.

    In addition, NVIDIA's cloud service agreements and data center leasing commitments have increased from $74 billion to $102 billion, further highlighting its intention to become the core of AI physical infrastructure.

    The CFO's remarks also disclosed a $105 billion guarantee related to a large OpenAI infrastructure project in Ohio. Storage Bets: $390 Billion AI GPUs heavily rely on high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is expensive and difficult to mass-produce. Meanwhile, Nvidia also has large projects that have just started, such as Blackwell and Vera Rubin.

    Therefore, Nvidia has signed multi-year procurement commitments of $390 billion for this type of storage to ensure its supply leadership.

    The main risk here is simple: once AI infrastructure and storage demand declines, Nvidia will be burdened with a large number of unnecessary bills; but apart from that, Nvidia's strategic intentions have been clearly expressed.

    So, what do you think Nvidia will look like in the post-Huang Renxun era?

data.title: When Intelligence Begins Mass Production: Six Trends in Large-Scale Models as Seen from Anthropic's Launch
data.description:
Author: Wang Qiang, Director of the Frontier Technology Research Center, Tencent Research Institute

Tonight, Anthropic, a company less than six years old, will be listed on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. Its speed and scale of development are nothing short of a miracle in technological and commercial history, offering a glimpse into the enormous impact of AI on the future economy and society.

Based on the final offering price of $83 per share, its fully diluted valuation is approximately $1.5 trillion. According to current expectations, its market capitalization may exceed $2 trillion after the IPO. Seven upstream companies—Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC—also subscribed for $26 billion. Its offering size surpasses SpaceX's initial public offering of $75 billion in June of this year, ranking among the largest IPOs in US stock market history.

Even more noteworthy than its valuation is its growth curve.

This continuous tenfold growth, far exceeding the rapid growth of the mobile internet era, has demonstrated the astonishing acceleration of AI to the world. In the first quarter of 2023, Claude began commercialization, starting with zero revenue. Its total revenue for 2023 was $41 million, $386 million in 2024, and $4.585 billion in 2025. By the third quarter of 2026, its single-quarter revenue reached $16.96 billion, 12.3 times that of the same period last year. Its annualized revenue in October of this year had already reached approximately $81 billion, and it is predicted that it could reach $100-120 billion by the end of the year. On the second page of the investor presentation materials, there's a sentence that reads: "For the first time in human history, intelligence has become something that humans can build. Cognitive abilities such as reasoning, analysis, synthesis, decision-making, and creation can be mass-produced and acquired on demand." I read this sentence several times. It's not actually talking about a company, but a turning point for an industry: for the first time, intelligence has begun to exist independently of humans, becoming an industrial product that can be mass-produced, priced, and scheduled. Especially the following image, which shows Anthropic's ambition. The returns it expects go far beyond current revenue from programming, analysis, and office work, extending to fields such as drug discovery, materials science, advanced manufacturing, robotics, and the $2 trillion life sciences market, and even the future $40 trillion global knowledge work market. This inevitably reminds us of a controversial rumor circulating in the industry: "In the future, there may only be one company left in the world, Anthropic." Over the past week, we've read through Anthropic's over 400-page prospectus, 15 pages of investor materials from its roadshow, 41 minutes of roadshow video, and an open letter signed by its seven founders. For the first time, a cutting-edge modeling company has fully disclosed how revenue is generated, where computing power is spent, how models iterate, how the organization operates, and how risks are priced. We can see six changes taking place in the large-scale modeling industry. Trend 1: The Scaling Law Still Holds Validity, But the Main Engine of R&D Has Shifted to AI Itself. Among Anthropic's founding team are the main authors of the 2020 paper "The Scaling Law of Neural Language Models." In their founder's letter, they stated that many people at the time didn't believe machine intelligence would be so heavily reliant on scale, but predictions based on the Scaling Law have been proven correct time and again. The prospectus also clearly states: AI capabilities will continue to improve, and in the foreseeable future, demand will continue to exceed supply, with supply primarily constrained by computing power. However, after reading the entire prospectus, I think what's more noteworthy is not the Scaling Law itself, but rather three changes in R&D methods. First, post-training has become the area with the largest investment. The prospectus states that post-training has evolved from a finishing step into one of the company's largest areas of research investment because the market is shifting from conversational assistants to autonomous intelligent agents. The training method has also changed, using complete, realistic tasks with a complexity approaching that of professional jobs. Anthropic believes that the breadth and realism of this task set is one of its most enduring scientific advantages, and it is difficult to observe from the outside, making it difficult to replicate. Secondly, the model architecture and inference infrastructure are designed together. AI researchers and inference engineers share planning cycles, reporting lines, and performance goals, and the architectural decisions take inference costs into account from day one. This explains why each generation of Claude can be both stronger and more cost-effective. Thirdly, and most importantly, AI is beginning to participate in building AI, which is currently the most discussed topic: RSI (Reference-Based Inference). Each generation of Claude participates in building the next generation, including running experiments, generating and processing training data, automating evaluation and security audits, writing code, and reviewing code. Several figures speak volumes. In September 2026, over 90% of commits to the Anthropic codebase were written by Claude; the daily code contribution per engineer in the third quarter was more than 45 times the average daily level in 2024. In open-ended engineering challenges lacking clear specifications and previously heavily reliant on the judgment of senior engineers, Claude's success rate improved by approximately 50 percentage points in nine months, reaching approximately 90%, according to internal benchmarks. When integrating AMD chips this year, Claude completed the adaptation within three days with minimal intervention, porting or writing almost all operators—something that previously required dozens of engineers several months. Based on the listed price, the value of using Claude internally at Anthropic increased more than 250 times from January to September of this year. In April of this year, this monthly value exceeded the company's monthly personnel expenses (excluding equity incentives) for the first time.

Image source: Anthropic roadshow investor materials

There is another trade-off that is easily overlooked. The prospectus explicitly states that although video and image generation models have commercial appeal, the company is not currently focused on them, and the corresponding computing power is being invested in programming, intelligent agents, and security research. There are three reasons: programming has a significant economic impact; security issues will first surface here; and the output of programming is largely verifiable.

The key to winning in the competition for large models is shifting to the speed of the R&D cycle. Whoever's model can perform its own company's work best first will see its next-generation model arrive faster. Verifiable areas will be conquered first and will also be the first to feed back into R&D. Of course, this cycle also has another side. The prospectus specifically mentions that accelerating AI with AI brings considerable security risks, and the company's responsible scaling policy already includes monitoring and mitigation plans for near-recursive self-improvement. The founder's letter puts it more directly: the company may proactively slow down if necessary. Trend Two: Products are moving from dialog boxes to virtual collaborators, delivering work rather than answers. The founder's letter includes a prediction of product generations: AI chatbots will become available around 2022, AI programmable agents around 2025, and agents for general knowledge work and scientific discovery will gradually become available around 2026. The letter also states that Anthropic will spend less effort consolidating existing products and more effort defining new products, because next-generation models always open up product categories that were not feasible just a few months ago. The prospectus names this generation of products "Virtual Collaborator": It possesses organizationally granted permissions, system connectivity, and context; it can use internal tools; it can execute multi-step workflows requiring continuous reasoning; and it works alongside employees. (Image source: Anthropic roadshow investor materials) Programming was the first category to cross the threshold. Claude Code was released as a research preview in February 2025. In about a year, Claude evolved from suggesting single lines of code to operating clusters of intelligent agents that autonomously work within production codebases. The prospectus compares the impact of Claude Code to the first widely adopted conversational AI assistants. Its uses are often unexpected; for example, NASA engineers used it to plan and write navigation instructions for the Mars Perseverance rover, completing the first AI-planned journey on Mars. Cybersecurity is perhaps the second. On a vulnerability exploitation benchmark developed by researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, Claude's score rose from 40% to 78%, and then to 91% in about four months. Knowledge work is the third. A sentence in the prospectus stuck with me: all digital work is ultimately a form of code expression. Based on this judgment, Anthropic adapted Claude Code's intelligent agent architecture to knowledge workers, creating Cowork, which autonomously reads files, operates applications, and executes multi-step workflows on the user's desktop, with the underlying code hidden. Cowork released a research preview in January 2026, and by the end of September, its adoption rate had surpassed that of Claude Code at the same point in time. In September, Cowork began merging with Claude.ai, allowing users to transition directly from simple questions to complex multi-step tasks within the same conversation. Dialogue and intelligent agents are being merged into a single product. Customer case studies also confirm this. Rakuten achieved over 7 hours of independent programming using Claude Code, reducing new feature launch time from 24 working days to 5; Salesforce completed an API migration that originally required 231 days in 13 days; Bristol-Myers Squibb's 30,000 employees all became proficient in Claude, reducing the response time for an epidemiological question from one or two months to four or five minutes. The product form has changed, and the technology stack must change accordingly. The prospectus contains a very simple statement: a model alone does not constitute an intelligent agent. For agents to recover from crashes, operate systems with limited, auditable credentials, and scale under varying loads, a runtime framework is essential. Anthropic has released the same runtime framework driving Claude Code as its Agent SDK, and also launched a managed version called Managed Agents. Combined with Agent Skills, the MCP protocol connecting enterprise data and tools, and the Model Hardware Standard (MHS) that allows agents to operate lab and manufacturing equipment, this forms the middle platform layer. The benefits of working with the model, platform, and application layers together are already evident in customer data. As of the end of September this year, more than half of customers with annual payments exceeding $100,000 were simultaneously using the platform and at least one first-party application, compared to approximately 30% in the fourth quarter of last year. The product unit for large models is shifting from a single response to a complete delivery. The focus of competition will shift from model performance metrics to engineering capabilities such as runtime frameworks, context management, permission systems, and tool connectivity—what's commonly referred to as Harness. Another noteworthy approach is that Anthropic designs its products around the capabilities the model will eventually possess, rather than around its current capabilities. Claude Code did just that, allowing the product to scale rapidly once the capabilities were in place. Trend Three: Pay-as-you-go, Models Have a Shelf Life Like Fresh Produce. Anthropic calls its main revenue model Pay-as-you-go, meaning billing based on usage, measured in tokens, and priced according to the selected model. In the first three quarters of 2026, usage-based billing accounted for 79% of revenue, subscriptions for 21%; revenue from the three major cloud platform markets accounted for 44%; and revenue from outside the US accounted for 29%. Three details particularly illustrate the characteristics of this model. First, the price reduction is about increasing sales volume, not waging a price war. In November 2025, Anthropic released Opus 4.5, which is more powerful, cheaper, and has lower per-task costs. Afterward, the company's revenue growth jumped from 48% in the fourth quarter of last year to 132% in the first quarter of this year. Opus 5.5, released in September this year, reduced the cost for customers to complete the same task by about 40%; Fable 5.1 reduced costs by about 25% compared to the previous generation, with savings of up to 45% for complex programming and highly agent-based tasks. According to the roadshow disclosures, the company lost about $600 million in revenue in the third quarter due to price reductions and contract discounts, but this was completely offset by increased usage. Management stated that the price reduction was neutral on profit margins because the new model itself requires less computing power. In other words, the decrease in token price reflects an efficiency advantage; improved computing efficiency precedes price reductions, which in turn stimulates further demand. Secondly, models have a shelf life. The prospectus discloses that over 80% of revenue in the third quarter came from model versions released within the past six months. In the first three quarters of this year, the company launched 250 new model versions, platform features, and applications. In this industry, models are not software developed once and sold long-term; they are more like fresh produce requiring continuous updates. If one stops, customers will migrate to someone else's latest model. Thirdly, revenue follows the pace of employee work. The prospectus mentions that in the two weeks ending January 2nd of this year, total customer spending decreased by approximately 20% compared to the previous two weeks. This was due to many companies implementing code freezes during holidays, slowing down code submissions and feature deployments by developers. The revenue of an AI company is beginning to show seasonality similar to that of the human resources service industry. This indirectly illustrates that Claude has deeply embedded itself in real-world production activities. Another commitment worth mentioning is that Claude does not advertise. The founder's letter states that advertising is likely to be a substantial source of revenue, but once advertising reaches revenue targets, the pressure to increase user engagement time will rise. The company hopes that Claude's sole incentive will be to provide users with a useful answer. The revenue model determines the product's incentive direction, a point applicable to all companies developing intelligent agents. The pricing unit for large models is shifting from seats to tokens, and the next step may be tasks and results. Whoever can continuously reduce the cost per task will benefit from demand elasticity; and whether the cost per task can be reduced depends on the computing power efficiency discussed below. Trend 4: Enterprises are the main battleground, developers are the entry point, and delivery capability is the new bottleneck. Anthropic has focused on enterprises from the very beginning. The founders believe that the enormous value of AI primarily comes from how enterprises and organizations deploy it. The numbers are growing rapidly. The number of customers paying over $100,000 annually was approximately 20 by the end of 2023, approximately 200 by the end of 2024, over 950 by September 2025, and over 11,900 by the end of September this year—a 12-fold increase in one year. Among them, over 1,900 have annual payments exceeding $1 million, and approximately 250 have payments exceeding $10 million. The net revenue retention rate is approximately 900%, meaning that customers who have been paying for Claude for a year spent about nine times more this quarter than in the same period a year ago. The customer structure is also becoming healthier. The revenue share of the top five customers decreased from 36% in the first quarter of this year to 21% in the third quarter, with no single customer accounting for more than 10%. More importantly, there is still significant room for growth. More than half of the Fortune 500 companies are already paying customers with annual fees exceeding $100,000, but these customers' average spending on Claude is less than 0.1% of their total expenses; even the top ten spenders spend less than 1%. The prospectus states that the gap between what Claude can do and its widespread use is one of the company's biggest growth opportunities. How is the money spent? The roadshow described the typical path as four steps: engineers first use Claude Code, then extend it to adjacent roles, then into business processes, and finally embed it into external products. The prospectus provides a comparison: In the third quarter, enterprise users who didn't use Claude Code spent an average of less than $75 per month, while the top 5% of Claude Code users spent approximately 20 times more. Developers are both the most discerning early adopters and the most persuasive promoters within enterprises. However, bottom-up approaches alone are not enough. The prospectus acknowledges that a major obstacle to Claude's adoption is the inherent resistance to change within organizations. To this end, Anthropic has built a complete delivery system: its direct sales team and application AI team are organized by region and then by industry, working with customers to design and deploy customized solutions; it collaborates with the three major cloud providers—AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure—for joint sales, with customers signing contracts directly with Anthropic and Anthropic paying the cloud providers; system integrators such as Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG, and PwC have formed dedicated Claude business teams; its partner network has certified over 150,000 professionals from more than 4,000 organizations; in October, it invested $100 million to establish an academy, planning to train 10,000 FDE engineers by the end of 2027 to bring AI to production environments according to its own engineer standards; and it has also partnered with private equity firms to establish an AI services company specifically for mid-sized enterprises. Even so, in the first half of this year, sales, marketing, and partner expenses only accounted for 19% of revenue. Model capabilities have already outpaced organizational absorption capabilities. The next bottleneck for enterprise AI is not in models, but in delivery: FDE engineers, application teams, and ecosystem partners who can integrate models into real business processes will become the most scarce resources. This is the same thing we observed previously: the number of field delivery engineers increased 15 times in one year. Trend Five: Computing power is the biggest cost, and also a futures contract spanning multiple periods. First, look at efficiency. From Q1 2025 to Q3 2026, Anthropic's revenue increased 45 times, while computing power and infrastructure spending only increased 10.4 times. The revenue generated from every $1 spent on computing power rose from $0.40 to $1.72, reaching as high as $2.08 in Q2. Image source: Anthropic roadshow investor materials. The company gave two reasons. First, the algorithm improvement led to a doubling of computing power, allowing the same model to be trained and run with less computing power. Second, the multi-chip architecture: training and inference are performed simultaneously on Amazon Trainium, Google TPU, NVIDIA GPU, and AMD GPU. All computing power is treated as an interchangeable resource pool and uniformly allocated, with computing power allocated to the location with the highest marginal output. The aforementioned three-day access to AMD is the result of this capability and closed-loop system. Now let's look at the mismatch. The prospectus states that the company typically purchases computing power 12 to 18 months in advance. This cost is basically fixed in the short term, while demand doubles every quarter. The result was that profits fluctuated significantly with demand forecasts. In the second quarter, revenue outpaced the computing power contracts signed more than a year prior, with computing power expenditures accounting for only 48% of revenue. Operating profit turned positive for the first time among the disclosed quarters, with an operating profit margin of 8%. In the third quarter, demand continued to surge, and the company purchased $5 billion worth of short-term computing power at a high price, significantly higher than multi-year contracts. This accounted for about half of the computing power expenditures in that quarter, bringing the computing power share back to 58%, and the operating profit margin turned negative 3%. Another set of figures is worth comparing. According to the roadshow presentation, the gross profit margin for the first three quarters of this year was 85%, but if all computing power expenditures, including model training, are excluded, the profit margin is only 43%. The gross profit margin only includes the computing power used to serve customers; the computing power used to train the next generation of models is not included. For large-scale companies, the real bulk of costs lies outside of gross margin. Finally, consider scale. As of the end of September and beyond, Anthropic has signed computing power and infrastructure commitments of approximately $900 billion, of which approximately $451.6 billion will occur before the end of 2030, with the remainder primarily between 2031 and 2045. The approximately $70.7 billion due in the next 12 months is lower than the current annualized revenue of approximately $81 billion; however, the portion before the end of 2030 is already 5.6 times the current annualized revenue. To have more room to maneuver in this intertemporal game, Anthropic is shifting more computing power to its self-built system, Anthropic Direct: leasing its own chips and placing them in dedicated data centers built to its own specifications. Its brilliance lies in separating two things: data center construction has a long cycle, but only accounts for a small portion of the total cost, so it can be locked in upfront; chip investment is large, and the amount to be purchased can be decided when demand is clearer. Management's long-term goal is to reduce computing power expenditure to 45% to 50% of revenue, with an adjusted operating profit margin exceeding 35%. The founder's letter is very frank about this: the company often makes seemingly irresponsible forward-looking investments, especially in computing power. The letter uses the pharmaceutical industry as an analogy, where early R&D investment is huge, and the returns only become worthwhile once a successful drug is developed; however, this process is faster and on a larger scale in AI. At the same time, the company is willing to forgo some upside potential in exchange for downside protection, such as selling excess computing power when demand is overestimated, continuously improving efficiency to increase tolerance for misjudgments, and raising funds in advance when necessary. In the letter's words, be bold, but be clear-headed. The core operational capabilities of large-scale model companies are beginning to become demand forecasting and computing power scheduling. To assess a heavily invested AI company, first look at its output per unit of computing power, then examine whether the duration of its computing power contracts matches the growth rate of demand. The former determines whether it can make money, while the latter determines whether it will be overwhelmed by computing power costs in a given quarter. Trend Six: Security and Governance, From Cost Centers to Part of the Product In April of this year, Anthropic trained its then-most powerful model, Mythos. Determined that its ability to discover network vulnerabilities was too strong, it didn't release it fully immediately. Instead, through a program called Project Glasswing, it provided a limited research preview to select organizations for cybersecurity defense, while also granting approximately $100 million in usage credits to those providing the defense. Only after adding additional security measures did the company fully release it in June under the name Fable 5. The founder admitted that this delay meant giving up considerable revenue and relinquishing some competitive position. Was this commercially worthwhile? The prospectus answers this by stating that rigorous security measures, predictable model behavior, and provable accountability have become decisive criteria for enterprises selecting AI partners for mission-critical tasks. Well-aligned models are better at following instructions, less likely to perform destructive actions without understanding user intent, and are more resistant to injection attacks. When models begin to integrate into critical business systems as intelligent agents, security equates to reliability, and reliability determines marketability. To this end, Anthropic has partnered with over 100 clients in the financial, healthcare, and public sectors to develop cutting-edge enterprise-grade security: monitoring data is stored in the client's own cloud account, encrypted with the client's keys, and abuse alerts are sent directly to the client's security team, without the involvement of Anthropic employees. In terms of governance, Anthropic is a Delaware-based non-profit corporation, and its board of directors must balance shareholder interests with its philanthropic mission. Power is shared by three parties: the seven co-founders hold a fixed 50.1% voting right through one Class F share, electing three directors; a long-term interest trust with no financial interest in the company elects four of the seven directors, with a protection mechanism in place for the nomination and removal of one of the directors, allowing employee votes in case of disagreement between the company and the trust. The founders' special voting rights are not permanent; if there are fewer than three founders in the voting entity, the rights revert to ordinary shareholders. Philanthropic arrangements are also enshrined in the equity: 5% of the equity is allocated to establish a philanthropic fund before the IPO, and the board can allocate an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the share price thereafter. All seven co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their personal equity, and over half of the employees also pledged to donate a portion of their equity. There's a passage in the founders' letter that I think is the most sobering part of the entire IPO filing. They said that before launching the IPO, they consulted many entrepreneurs who had gone public, and several gave similar advice: never let your company be worth even a dollar more than its actual value. Because it's very dangerous when people buy stock based on expectations you can't deliver, or misjudge how you'll act. Therefore, the letter specifically outlined two types of decisions the company might make that might go against investor expectations: one is a business bet stemming from the exponential growth of AI that seems somewhat abnormal on its own, and the other is a choice that deviates from profit maximization to balance the public interest. Security is also a key factor in Anthropic's success in attracting talent. All seven co-founders remain with the company, with an unexpected turnover rate of about 1%. Of the employees the company wanted to retain but left, 19% later returned; over three-quarters of the first 100 employees are still with the company. When the model evolves from answering questions to acting on behalf of others, trust becomes an integral part of the product's functionality. Security investment is no longer just a compliance cost, but a payment for critical business access for enterprise clients. Four uncertainties in the prospectus also warrant attention: First, growth is bound to slow. Third-quarter growth was 47%, significantly lower than the 144% in the second quarter. The prospectus itself clearly states that revenue growth will decline over time, and the decline may be larger and faster than expected; as growth slows, seasonal fluctuations will become more pronounced, and performance will be more difficult to predict. Second, revenue quality. The prospectus discloses that approximately 5% to 7% of revenue in the first nine months of this year came from clients subsequently found to have violated usage policies or business terms. The company strengthened monitoring and enforcement in August and September, and this portion of revenue will gradually decrease, but the extent and timing of its impact on growth are currently uncertain. Third, there is a mismatch in computing power. The approximately $900 billion commitment must generally be fulfilled regardless of revenue and utilization rates. Part of the computing power construction also relies on funding or credit support from cloud vendors and chip partners. Amazon and Google are both major shareholders with stakes exceeding 5%, and are also customers, distribution channels, and competitors; this multifaceted relationship inherently introduces uncertainty. Fourth, there are book losses. The net loss in the third quarter was $23.3 billion, of which $21.9 billion was due to changes in the fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFE resulting from valuation increases—non-cash items; however, equity incentive expenses recognized after the IPO will continue to weigh on the profit and loss statement. In terms of competition, OpenAI, Google, and the continuously improving Open Weights model are all on the same track. From the IPO pricing perspective, the market has already factored this in. Five Insights for the Large Model Industry By combining these six trends, we can derive five insights for the industry. First, in R&D, become the primary user of your own model. Anthropic's closed-loop model demonstrates that the depth of internal usage is a greater determinant of iteration speed than external rankings. Start with verifiable areas like code, allowing the model to first transform its own R&D process, and then spill over this capability to customers. Second, in product development, shift from dialogue to delivery. Models, operating frameworks, connection protocols, and skill sets should be developed together, designing products around deliverables rather than the quality of responses; simultaneously, plan products based on the model's capabilities six months from now, rather than focusing solely on current capabilities. Third, in business, treat output per unit of computing power as the primary business metric. A pay-as-you-go model with continuous price reductions presupposes a continuous decrease in the cost per task. Price reductions without efficiency improvements are merely subsidies; only price reductions supported by efficiency improvements can generate demand elasticity. Fourth, in the market, enterprise services compete on delivery systems. Bottom-up penetration by developers, deep delivery by AI application teams, ecosystem coverage by cloud platforms and integrators, FDE engineer certification and training, and service models geared towards medium-sized enterprises are all indispensable. When model capabilities are abundant, whoever can translate those capabilities into results within the customer's workflow will generate revenue. Fifth, in terms of computing power, heterogeneous computing power pooling and long-term/short-term combinations are fundamental. A model company's ability to efficiently train and infer on multiple chips, to automatically port operators using AI, and to separately lock in data centers and chips, and to effectively combine long-term and short-term contracts, directly determines its profit elasticity during demand fluctuations. This is particularly relevant for companies that need to run models on multiple chips simultaneously. Finally, let's return to that point: Never let your company be worth even a dollar more than its actual value. The significance of Anthropic's IPO isn't just about adding another trillion-dollar company to the list, but about the fact that for the first time, the large-scale model industry is facing quarterly reconciliation in the public market. After intelligent models begin mass production, what's more difficult than creating smarter models is consistently proving that someone is willing to pay for the intelligence gained from each unit of computing power. This test begins tonight, November 19th, when the market opens.

data.title: Abu Dhabi Court Orders 18 Crypto Firms Including Circle and World Liberty Financial to Keep Stolen Binance Tokens Frozen
data.description:
Abu Dhabi Judges Move to Lock Down Billions in Stolen Binance Crypto

Stolen digital tokens worth billions of dollars now sit under a court-ordered freeze in Abu Dhabi, as Binance pushes to claw back what thieves took from its wallets.

The Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM) Courts have told 18 crypto firms, including Circle and World Liberty Financial, to keep their hold on tokens linked to the theft.

The raid on 29 October 2026 drained about $6.3 billion from Binance wallets, making it the largest crypto heist on record.

🚨BINANCE SAYS IT HAS COURT ORDER FROM ABU DHABI TO RECOVER FROZEN TOKENS FROM RECENT HACK!@binance says it secured a court order from the Abu Dhabi Global Market as part of its efforts to recover tokens that were frozen after the big hack, according to Reuters.

The exchange… pic.twitter.com/crfynagH2N

— Crypto Banter (@crypto_banter) November 18, 2026

Who Has Been Told to Keep the Tokens Frozen?

Circle, which issues the dollar-linked stablecoin USDC, and World Liberty Financial, the crypto venture run by the family of US President Donald Trump, head the list of named companies.

The court was careful to say that none of the 18 firms is accused of wrongdoing.

Many had already frozen the tokens before the order arrived.

Under the ruling, they must maintain those freezes until further proceedings.

They are also barred from lending or swapping the tokens, or mixing them with other assets.

The order is an interim measure to protect assets Binance says belong to it, and it does not decide who finally gets the money back.

A further hearing on 1 December 2026 will weigh whether the injunction should continue and on what terms.

Binance recovery: An Abu Dhabi court ordered 18 cryptocurrency companies to preserve frozen assets connected to October's $6.3 billion Binance wallet theft. Binance says approximately $2.85 billion has been frozen or intercepted.

— Fizy Xchange💙🦅 (@FizyXchange) November 19, 2026

Why Is Tether Missing From the Order?

Tether, the El Salvador-based issuer of the USDT token, is not among the named companies, even though it earlier said it had frozen $1.5 billion of the stolen funds.

Binance says it is working with Tether directly on returning those assets.

A Tether spokesperson said:

"In consultation with the relevant authorities, we will work directly with Binance in respect of reissuing the tokens."

Binance said on 3 November that around $2.85 billion of the stolen tokens had been frozen or intercepted by third parties.

Stablecoins from Tether and Circle can be frozen by their issuers, but bitcoin is far harder to pull back once it moves, unless it lands at an exchange or service willing to cooperate.

How Big Is the Wider Court Package?

A separate account of the proceedings describes a much larger set of orders.

According to it, Justice William Stone SBS KC granted a worldwide freezing injunction with a stated value of $6.5 billion against unidentified people alleged to have carried out the fraud.

That figure is the amount covered by the order, not money already recovered.

Binance has not said how much of the stolen crypto has come back through the court action.

The package also includes interim proprietary injunctions and delivery-up orders against different groups of unidentified defendants, plus interim orders against named defendants that had frozen some of the assets.

Gibson Dunn, the US law firm acting for Binance, called the injunction "one of, if not the, largest publicly known freezing orders ever made."

Can a Court Order Chase Stolen Crypto Across Blockchains?

The orders try to answer that with technology.

They allow court papers to be served through the blockchain itself, and they rely on a constantly updated "living list" of about 26,000 wallet addresses said to hold stolen assets.

🚨 BINANCE JUST WON A 6.5BILLIONFREEZEORDER!

⚖️AbuDhabi'sADGMCourtsissuedaworldwidefreezinginjunctionagainsttheunknownOct29hackers
🔗Itcoversa"livinglist"of~26,000walletsandcanbeservedON-CHAIN
🧊~2.85B of the ~$6.34B stolen was already frozen… pic.twitter.com/OQuj0wYfcC

— BodLaim (@Bodlaim_) November 19, 2026

M. Kendall Day of Gibson Dunn explained:

"Just as significant is how the orders will work in practice: they can be served via the blockchain, and the market will be notified of a constantly updating 'living list' of 26,000 wallet addresses identified as holding stolen assets, enabling those assets to be frozen rapidly even as they are laundered at pace."

The paperwork also matters for a practical reason.

Some issuers and exchanges need formal judicial approval before they release or return frozen funds, and the ADGM orders give them that cover.

🔰 BINANCE STRIKES BACK! A $6.5 BILLION GLOBAL FREEZING ORDER!

There's a major breakthrough in the aftermath of the October 29 hack.@binance has secured a worldwide asset-freezing injunction from Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM) Courts, covering up to $6.5 BILLION in assets… https://t.co/YncIgBiLBxpic.twitter.com/8vAby8VRVM

— FrontierX 🔶 (@RealFrontierX) November 19, 2026

What Does Binance Say About Its Customers?

Binance says users have not lost out.

The company covered the stolen assets from its own reserves, including its emergency fund SAFU and its corporate treasury, and has resumed withdrawals in phases.

Dugan Bliss, the firm's deputy general counsel, said:

"We will continue using every lawful tool available to trace, freeze and recover stolen assets, support our partners in returning funds where possible, and keep those assets out of the hands of the attackers."

Abu Dhabi is Binance's global hub, and the company counts the ADGM's Financial Services Regulatory Authority as its main regulator.

SB Seker, its Asia-Pacific head, told the Singapore Fintech Festival that the company plans to enter five Asian markets in 2027 and needs no new fundraising after the hack.

"The cost of covering the stolen tokens is not a large amount for us statistically. The impact is manageable, and we can get through it without changing how we operate."

Talks with three of those markets are nearing the final stage, with details due in the first quarter of 2027.

How Did the Attackers Get In?

Binance says the attack took months to prepare.

In June, tampered software in an installer compromised an engineer's device.

In September, another engineer was approached by someone posing as a recruiter and was tricked into running a fake interview task that carried malware.

The attackers then reached the company's internal wallet-signing service and, on 29 October, emptied hot wallets across several blockchains.

The haul included about 233.46 million XRP, about 975,000 SOL and about 18,270 BTC.

Binance says it has covered every asset hit by the 29 October hack. It paid for that out of its own funds.

Getting the stolen coins back is a separate track. Binance's blog of 3 November puts the impact at about 6.34billion,including18,270BTC and 233.46 million $XRP sent… pic.twitter.com/rIl630RxA0

— Yieldr.io (@yieldr_official) November 14, 2026

Blockchain analysis suggests the thieves tried to swap stablecoins into ether quickly but could not outrun the issuers' freezes.

The FBI and Binance have both pointed to North Korea's "TraderTraitor" group, while Pyongyang has denied any role.

Could This Case Become a Template for the Industry?

Stablecoin issuers have frozen assets at the request of authorities before, but a court ordering many firms to hold a freeze at once is unusual.

Market watchers see the Abu Dhabi order as a possible model for protecting assets after future thefts.

It also shows how hard it remains to recover decentralised assets such as bitcoin.

For Binance, much now rests on the 1 December hearing and on how many of the frozen tokens can be returned.

data.title: Anthropic's IPO is finally complete: valuation reaches $1.5 trillion.
data.description:
Anthropic's IPO price was set at $83, valuing the company at approximately $1.5 trillion. Excluding the transfer of existing shares, the company expects to raise approximately $79 billion, surpassing SpaceX to become the largest IPO in history. The stock will begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol "ANT".

On Wednesday evening local time, Anthropic announced that the IPO would sell 155 million more shares than initially expected, expanding its already record-breaking IPO size by nearly $13 billion.

The AI ​​lab will issue a total of 980 million shares, compared to 825 million shares in its latest prospectus.

Anthropic's IPO price was set at $83, higher than the previously indicated range of $70-$78. Trading began on Thursday under the ticker symbol "ANT". On a fully diluted basis, the offering is expected to value the company at approximately $1.5 trillion. In line with market expectations, only a small portion of the shares (approximately 23.6 million shares) came from existing shareholders. Excluding the transfer of existing shares, the company expects to raise approximately $79 billion, surpassing SpaceX to become the largest IPO in history. In June, SpaceX issued 555.6 million shares at $135, raising $75 billion. In addition to this $79 billion, Anthropic is expected to complete a $26 billion private placement (subscribed by Nvidia, Google, Microsoft, Micron, AMD, TSMC, and Broadcom), bringing its total post-IPO fundraising to $105 billion. Furthermore, the underwriting banks have an over-allotment option to purchase additional shares. This major IPO is even bigger than before. Anthropic: The First Pure AI Lab to Go Public on the US Stock Market. While many other publicly traded companies, including Meta, Alphabet, and SpaceX, are developing large-scale AI models, Anthropic will become the first company whose entire business revolves around AI research and development. The company continuously iterates and upgrades the Claude model, providing services through its own platform and third-party cloud vendors, and developing various application products based on the model. This cycle continues. Dan Ives, a technology analyst who is bullish on AI, wrote in a research report on Wednesday: "This is the first time a leading US AI lab has had an independent public market valuation." He added that this valuation "has not been muddied by its advertising or rocket business." Anthropic is unlikely to remain alone for long; its main competitor, OpenAI, has also filed confidential IPO documents with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), but is not expected to go public until 2027. Anthropic shares have been "frozen" for some time. The biggest winners of Anthropic's rapid growth are the early investors who entered the market before its IPO. Since completing its Series G funding round in February at a valuation of $380 billion, Anthropic's market capitalization has almost quadrupled. However, investors wanting to buy and sell shares before the IPO have not had an easy time. Several private equity firms have stated that their private trading activity has been very quiet in recent months. Anthropic explicitly stated in May that it would not approve any share transfers without the company's approval. Greg Martin, managing director of private brokerage firm Rainmaker Securities, said this warning was like "pouring cold water" on over-the-counter trading. “If you’re a buyer, you don’t want to buy something that isn’t recognized,” Martin told Barron’s; and if you’re a seller holding shares in this high-value company, “the last thing you want is to create complications.” Early investors’ shares will still be subject to a lock-up period of several months after the IPO, which is a standard IPO arrangement, but they are now one step closer to realizing their gains. The $1.5 trillion valuation is an equilibrium result of multiple parties’ negotiations. The $1.5 trillion valuation falls within a comfortable range between the upper and lower limits of investor expectations. This summer, there were rumors that its valuation could reach $2 trillion, but subsequently, the AI ​​sector weakened, and investors lowered their expectations. Anthropic itself remained silent on this matter until last week when it announced its offering price range of $70 to $78. The final IPO price of $83 indicates strong market demand for Anthropic stock, but the valuation wasn't so high as to deter potential investors. "I think this shows that people have a huge appetite for exposure to the long-term trend of 'smart' technology," said David Fetherstonhaugh, chief investment officer at asset management firm VistaShares, regarding the final pricing. Is Anthropic's stock price expensive? Currently, Wall Street's assessment of Anthropic is still limited. Investment banks involved in the IPO typically wait two to three weeks to release their research reports. Of course, brokerages not involved in the IPO can comment on the valuation. Pierre Ferragu, an analyst at New Street Research, has already initiated coverage. He predicts that Anthropic's EBITDA will reach $183 billion by 2030. Based on its IPO pricing, Anthropic's valuation is approximately 8 times its projected 2030 EBITDA. Whether this price is worthwhile is difficult to determine. In comparison, SpaceX's valuation is approximately 4 times its estimated 2030 EBITDA. The S&P 500's valuation is approximately 13 times its projected 12-month EBITDA. Currently, there is no reliable estimate of the S&P 500's 2030 EBITDA. The extremely high growth expectations provide some support for AI valuations, but 2030 is still a long way off, and the industry is changing rapidly. A key figure Anthropic investors should pay attention to: After its IPO, Anthropic will be required to disclose quarterly financial reports. Going forward, investors should closely monitor its "computing cost gross margin"—that is, the gross profit after deducting computing power costs. According to the prospectus, Anthropic's third-quarter revenue was approximately $17 billion, a year-on-year surge of 1127%; computing power investment was close to $10 billion, with a remaining profit of approximately $7.1 billion after deducting computing power costs, resulting in a computing power gross margin of 42%. In the second quarter, this gross margin was 52%. This stronger gross margin indicates strong pricing and demand for Anthropic's services; it also means that Anthropic needs more computing power—which is crucial for AI computing power service providers like SpaceX and CoreWeave. It's difficult to predict where the gross margin will ultimately stabilize. Finding companies with quarterly revenues of tens of billions of dollars and growth rates exceeding 1000% for comparison is not easy. Anthropic's IPO May Displace Nvidia's Leading Position in AI, Diverting Tech Funds

Market attention is entirely focused on Anthropic. Some investors believe that the upcoming IPO of Anthropic could replace Nvidia as the new leader in AI deals.

Typically, new stocks are not discussed in terms of whether they pose a significant challenge to established companies, especially when the competitor is a company with a peak market capitalization of nearly $5 trillion.

However, the resignation of Nvidia's founder and former CEO Jensen Huang due to scandal has prompted investors to speculate that Anthropic could become the new king of AI. If this prediction comes true, funds will be sold off from other tech stocks and used to increase holdings in Anthropic.

Some investors say that Nvidia's institutional shareholders (whether they have already reduced their holdings or still hold Nvidia positions) are eager to buy Anthropic shares.

An advisor who placed orders with clients for this IPO stated that the funds entering ANT must have a source, and the funds withdrawn from Nvidia seem to be a logical one. Amazon and Google hold large stakes, but their voting rights are not significant. Combined, Amazon and Google will likely hold more than 35% of Anthropic's shares in the future. After the IPO and concurrent private placement, Google will hold 1.8 billion shares. At $74 per share, this corresponds to an equity value of approximately $133 billion. Amazon initially holds 1.9 billion shares and also holds convertible bonds in Anthropic. If all of these are exercised and converted into shares, Amazon will hold a maximum of 3.5 billion shares, equivalent to a value of approximately $260 billion at $74 per share. Together, they represent 28.4% of the issued common stock; if Amazon converts all of its bonds, its combined shareholding is estimated to reach 36%. However, the significant shareholdings of the two companies do not grant them much formal governance power within Anthropic. Anthropic employs a complex shareholding structure, with the seven founders retaining a combined 50.1% of the voting rights. In most major votes, Class A shareholders, including existing shareholders and IPO new share buyers, hold only 49.9% of the voting rights. Amazon and Google hold Class N shares, specifically reserved for business partners. These shares do not have regular voting rights unless converted into Class A shares through sale or transfer. Nevertheless, these two companies remain deeply tied to Anthropic's success or failure, enjoying substantial economic benefits. Besides Google and Amazon, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC also participated in the subscription. Analysts: Anthropic is a "once-in-a-generation IPO" This AI company, backed by Claude's grand model, has already garnered bullish ratings from Wall Street institutions even before its IPO pricing has been finalized. New Street Research analyst Pierre Ferragu was the first to initiate coverage of Anthropic, giving it a "buy" rating and a target price of $105. This bullish report was released on the eve of Anthropic's listing. "Anthropic is a 'once-in-a-generation' IPO. We expect AI's share of knowledge work-related spending to continue to rise over the next few decades, just as cloud computing's share of IT spending has steadily increased since 2010," Ferragu said. In his view, the only difference is that AI "is adopting at twice the speed of cloud computing, and its potential market size is ten times larger." Ferragu estimates the current potential market size for AI to be $35 trillion, expanding to $50 trillion by 2030. He believes that Anthropic, with its self-developed AI models, is in a leading position in the industry and is expected to deliver solid operating results after its IPO. The analyst predicts that Anthropic's cash burn will remain low; revenue will reach $500 billion by 2030, with an EBIT margin of approximately 15%.
